sentences.text: Succinctly put, the case of the complainant is that he was appointed as Senior Sales Executive in a firm called Sakida Financial, started by the accused, one Mr. Bhupesh Madan and Standard Chartered Bank and had accrued business for the firm which entitled him to incentive of more than Rs. 1,00,000/- from the firm.

Despite repeated requests and demands, the incentive amount was not paid to the complainant by the accused on one pretext or another and he was maltreated, in front of the office staff, by the accused when the amount was demanded.

After being continuously harassed on the job, the complainant left his job with Sakida Financial on 30.09.2003 and demanded his salary due for the month of September, 2003 as well as the incentive amount due towards him.
However, the accused threatened to kill the complainant if the amount was demanded.

The KATYAYINI by KATYAYINI SHARMA SHARMA KANDWAL KANDWAL Date: 2024.07.15 16:24:01 +0530 accused also visited the office of complainant with two other persons who slapped him, held him by his neck and threatened to kill him if he ever approached the accused for money.
3. In view of the aforesaid facts, the complainant had filed a complaint case against the accused for commission of offence under section 406/420/323/506 of the IPC.
The accused was summoned by this Court vide order dated 23.06.2006 under section 406/323/506 Part II IPC.
Pre- charge evidence was led by the complainant.
Vide order dated 13.03.2020, the matter as put up for arguments on charge and vide order dated 12.05.2023, the accused was charged for offence under section 323/406/506 Part-II of the IPC.
The complainant adopted his pre-charge evidence as complainant evidence.

Matter was accordingly listed for recording of statement of accused under section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter "CrPC") which was recorded on Pawan Gupta vs Sanjeev Mahajan on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/178291896/
1 07.10.2023 where all incriminating evidence was put to the accused.
The accused did not lead defence evidence and the matter was listed for final arguments.
EVIDENCE 4.

Complainant was examined as PW-1 wherein he deposed that he was appointed as Senior Sales Executive in Saf Invest at the salary of Rs.5500/- per month and after issuance of appointment letter Ex. PW 1/1, he was to report to Mr. Bhupesh Madan, who was Assistant Manager in the Standard Chartered Bank.
The accused was employed as manager a Saf Invest.

That thereafter, the accused along with Mr. Bhupesh Madan and Standard Chartered Bank created a new firm by the name of Sakida Financial where the complainant was appointed as a Senior Sales Executive at the salary of KATYAYINI by KATYAYINI SHARMA SHARMA KANDWAL KANDWAL Date: 2024.07.15 16:24:16 +0530 Rs.5500/- p.m.
plus sales incentives and incentives at the rate 0.5% of the total business accrued by him were committed to the complainant.
The appointment letter of the complainant is Ex. PW1/2.

The complainant accrued a business around 2.5 crore during the period August, 2002 to September, 2003 but was not paid the promised incentive on one pretext or another and only a sum of Rs.42,000/- was paid to him though he was entitled for the incentive more than Rs.1,00,000/-.

The accused also gave an impression to the complainant that he received an email from Mr.
Bhupesh Madan and Mr. Sanjay Sehgal stating that the incentives of the complainant would be deducted for his Provident Fund (PF) after which his account will be cleared.

Despite repeated requests stating that the PF would be a small amount and to provide him with remaining balance of his incentive amount, the accused gave an impression that the incentive money of the complainant would be utilised for pleasing the officers of the bank and was maltreated by the accused in the presence of staff, if the amount was demanded.

After being continuously harassed on the job, the complainant left his job with Sakida Financial on 30.09.2003 and demanded his salary due for the month of September, 2003 as well as the incentive amount.
The accused got irritated at the demand of the complainant, threatened him to kill him to death and to falsely implicate him in false criminal cases.

The complainant thereafter talked to Mr. Bhupesh Madan and Mr. Sanjay Sehgal and after apprising them about the cheating meted out to him, he was informed that they had never sent any email to the accused regarding deduction of incentives for provident fund or for pleasing the officers of bank.

The complainant thereafter realised that the accused had concocted a story for cheating him and when the accused was again confronted for the salary and incentive amount, he threatened to kill the complainant to death.

The accused after getting KATYAYINI by KATYAYINI SHARMA KANDWAL KANDWAL Date: 2024.07.15 16:24:28 +0530 aggravated by repeated demands by the complainant for his salary and incentives came to the office of complainant with two goons who slapped him, held him by his neck and threatened to kill him if he ever approached the accused for money.
The accused also threatened the complainant that he has good connections with the police and that he would implicate the complainant in false cases, which scared the complainant.
It was stated that the complainant has not received his aforesaid legitimate dues as well as salary for the month of September, 2003 despite repeated request and demand from the accused.

5. Complainant has relied on the testimony of CW-2 who exhibited Ex. CW2/B and Ex. CW2/C to prove the business accrued by him at Sakida Financial and to prove that no email had been sent by CW-2 to the accused regarding deduction of the incentive of complainant.

The corresponding entries in the bank account of Sakida Financial Services have been proven vide testimony of CW-5, Sh. Abhishek Shrivastva from Standard Chartered Bank at points- A, B and C in Ex. CW 5/3.

Testimony of CW-4 Mr. Amir Ahmed Deputy Manager, ICICI Bank has been relied upon to prove typographical error in one figure wrongly stated by CW-3 in Ex. CW3/1.
7. CW-6, Mr. Jagdish Salwan, Manager, Citi Bank was examined to show the total outstanding of the accused towards the bank and show his previous conduct of not making payment of dues on time.
8. The accused did not lead defence evidence and therefore, no witnesses were examined on his behalf.

That the fact that incentive at the rate 0.5% was payable to the complainant is clearly established from the testimony of complainant which is corroborated by testimonies of CW-3, CW-4 and CW-5 which have been clearly admitted by the accused in his statement recorded under section 313 CrPC where he has stated that the documents exhibited by these witnesses are matter of record;

Counsel

argued:
a.

That the complainant has failed to prove his case and commission of offences that the accused is charged with, beyond reasonable doubt which is the burden of proof on him;

That even though the offences as alleged were cognizable in nature, no police complaint had been lodged by the complainant against the accused;
c.

That no definite rate of interest at which the incentives were to be paid to the complainant was decided between the complainant and the accused as is also clear from appointment letter Ex. PW1/2; d. That the complainant had left the job suddenly on 30.09.2003 without giving any notice to the accused and further, there is no proof of demand of salary or the incentive and that nothing has been brought on record in form of independent evidence like email, notice, letter etc. issued by the complainant to the accused demanding the salary or the incentive amount; e.

In view of the submissions made above and the material on record including the citations relied upon by the parties to which the Court has given thoughtful consideration, this Court shall now procced to consider each offence separately.

HURT 12. Section 323 provides punishment for voluntarily causing hurt which is defined in section 319 of the IPC as follows:
KATYAYINI by KATYAYINI SHARMA KANDWAL KANDWAL Date: 2024.07.15 16:25:05 +0530 Hurt.--Whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any Pawan Gupta vs Sanjeev Mahajan on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/178291896/
4 person is said to cause hurt.

13. Ld. Counsel for complainant while relying on judgment in State v. Abdul Rehman and Anr. in Crl. Case No. 4/2023 passed by Ld. ACMM-04, Rouse Avenue Courts, New Delhi dated 29.04.2023,
has stated that the testimony of complainant as CW-1 is sufficient to prove commission of offence punishable under section 323 of the IPC.

sentences.text: It was further submitted that the accused has not been able to disprove or discredit the testimony of the complainant.

14. Per contra, Ld. Counsel for accused has stated that the complainant has failed to prove the ingredients of offence punishable under section 323 of the IPC beyond reasonable doubt as is the burden on him.

He argued that there are several facets of the present case which raise reasonable doubts on the testimony of the complainant like no medical certificate on record to show that any "bodily pain, disease or infirmity" was caused to the complainant as well as no independent evidence led to this effect.
15. Section 134 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 provides that no particular number of witnesses shall, in any case, be required for proof of any fact.
Simply because there is statement of only one witness is not sufficient to discredit the testimony without considering the complete facts and circumstances of the case.
However, in the present case, this Court is of the opinion that the complainant has not been able to prove commission of offence under section 323 of the IPC.

16. In Lakshman Singh v. State of Bihar (2021) 9 SCC 191, Hon'ble Apex Court, even in the absence of any medical certificate had upheld the conviction of accused for offence punishable under section 323 of the IPC wherein it held:
 KATYAYINI KATYAYINI  SHARMA KANDWAL  KANDWAL Date: 2024.0  16:25:18 +05

entities.text: Lakshman Singh v. State of Bihar (2021) 9 SCC 191
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
"Applying the law laid down by this Court in the aforesaid decisions to the facts of the case on hand,
we see no reason to doubt the credibility and/or trustworthiness of PW1, PW3 & PW4 and more particularly PW5, PW8 & PW10, who are the injured witnesses.
All the witnesses are consistent in their statements and they have fully supported the case of the prosecution.

Under the circumstances, the courts below have not committed any error in convicting the accused, relying upon the depositions of PW1, PW3, PW4, PW5, PW8 & PW10"
17.

The facts of the present case, however, are distinguishable from the facts of State v. Abdul Rehman (supra) as in the given case, even though there was no medical certificate to substantiate the allegations qua offence under section 323 of the IPC, the testimony of the complainant was clearly supported by the chain of events thereafter wherein steps like prompt filing of police complaint by her, site plan prepared by the IO etc were taken.

Similarly, in Lakshman Singh (supra),

even though no medical certificate qua the injuries suffered by the victims was placed on record,
there were consistent testimonies of several witnesses wherein one of the them (PW- 8) was also treated at a government hospital.
18. In the present case, there is nothing on record which supports the version of complainant apart from his testimony.
No complaint qua alleged incident was registered by him with the police and no notice has been issued to the accused.

A reasonable man who has been beaten by a person who allegedly owes him certain lawful payments is expected to take steps like calling at the number 100 upon occurrence of such incident, lodging a police complaint if not an FIR etc.
None of these steps have been taken by KATYAYINI by KATYAYINI SHARMA KANDWAL KANDWAL
Date: 2024.07.15 16:25:34 +0530 the complainant whose testimony also does not find any support from any independent evidence placed on record.
19. For the aforementioned reasons, this Court is of the view that the complainant has failed to prove commission of offence under section 323 of the IPC.
CRIMINAL BREACH OF TRUST 20.
The offence under Section 406 IPC is committed when a person entrusted with the property of another, dishonestly retains or misappropriates the same without the consent of that other person.
So the primary ingredient to be proved by the prosecution is that there was "entrustment" of articles by the complainant to the accused.
21. Section 405 of the IPC defines the offence of criminal breach of trust and Section 406 of the IPC is the penal provision for the offence.

Section 405 IPC reads as follows:
"405. Criminal breach of trust.--Whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use that property, or dishonestly uses or disposes of that property in violation of any direction of law prescribing the mode in which such trust is to be discharged, or of any legal contract, express or implied, which he has made touching the discharge of such trust, or wilfully suffers any other person so to do, commits criminal breach of trust."
22.

The essential ingredients for an offence under Section 405 of the IPC are as under;
 KATYAYINI SHARMA  SHARMA KANDWAL  KANDWAL

Date:
 2024.07.15  16:25:45 +0530 Pawan Gupta vs Sanjeev Mahajan on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/178291896/
6

1) A person should have been entrusted with property or entrusted with dominion over property;
2) He should have dishonestly misappropriated or converted to his own use that property, or dishonestly used or disposed of that property or wilfully suffered any other person to do so; and 3) Such misappropriation, conversion, use or disposal should be in violation of any direction of laws prescribing the mode in which such trust is to be discharged, or of any legal contract which the person has made, touching the discharge of such trust."

23. Section 405 of the IPC thus envisages entrustment of property or dominion over property by the accused and dishonest misappropriation of it by him in violation of any direction of law prescribing the manner of discharge.
On the bedrock of the essential ingredients, it is pertinent to examine whether the evidence on record fulfils the said requisites.
24. The "entrustment" has to be proven by the complainant by placing on record independent evidence to this effect.
Complainant has relied on Ex. CW 3/1 to prove that he was awarded incentive at the rate of 0.5% of the total business accrued by him.

It has been submitted that from the testimony of complainant as CW-1 and the aforesaid documents, it is clear that the rate at which incentive were to be awarded to the complainant was 0.5% which the accused has unlawfully not paid on the pretext that it would be used for pleasing the officers of the bank and towards deduction of his PF amount and hence, the accused has committed an offence punishable under section 406 of the IPC.

It was also argued that the accused has not paid the salary due for the month of September 2003 to the complainant even though the complainant resigned on 30.09.2003 i.e. after working for the entirety of the given month.
KATYAYINI by KATYAYINI
SHARMA KANDWAL  KANDWAL

From the perusal of record, it is clear that the terms of employment of the complainant with Sakida Financial were provided in Ex. PW 1/2 wherein though it is mentioned that the incentive shall be awarded to the complainant, however, the exact rate at which the same was ought to be awarded is not provided.

Therefore, it is clear from the perusal of appointment letter that no rate of incentive was agreed upon between the parties, at the very least in writing in the contents of the aforementioned appointment letter.

The complainant has relied on Ex. CW2/B and Ex. CW2/C to argue that the awarded incentive for the months October 2002 to November 2002 was 0.53%
wherein Rs. 16175/- had been paid as incentive to the complainant who has accrued business of Rs.
30,08,000/- during the given period and therefore, it can be implied that agreed rate of interest of incentives was 0.5% of the total business accrued by the complainant.

The bank account statements of the complainant to prove the same is Ex. CW3/1 which is also corroborated by Ex. CW 5/1, Ex.
CW 5/2 and Ex. CW 5/3 collectively.

The accused has argued that the rate of incentive was never Pawan Gupta vs Sanjeev Mahajan on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/178291896/
7 agreed upon and that it could have changed as per the circumstances subsisting at the given time for instance, the sales carried out during the given period.
26.
It is reasonable that rate of incentive, unless clearly agreed upon, would depend on not only the business accrued by an employee but also the profits accrued to the company.
Therefore, there may be circumstances where even though the business of a company is growing but the simultaneous expenses not result in increase of profits of the company at the same rate.
Moreover, the complainant has not been able to lead any independent evidence in support of his claim.
As per section 103 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the burden of proof lies on the person who alleges some new facts.

In the present case, the fact that the complainant is alleging the he KATYAYINI by KATYAYINI SHARMA KANDWAL KANDWAL Date: 2024.07.15 16:26:15 +0530 was entitled to interest at the rate of 0.5% and therefore, the burden of proving the same beyond reasonable doubt was upon the complainant which he has failed to do.
The complainant could have examined the employees of Sakida Financial to establish the ordinary business practice regarding payment of incentives followed there.
Merely because incentive at the rate of 0.53% was paid for the business of October and November 2002 does not imply that the given percentage was agreed upon as the fixed rate of incentive.

Further, it has been admitted by the complainant, at the stage of final arguments,
that he was paid incentive at the rate 0.13% for December 2002 to March 2003, 0.21% for April 2003 to June 2003 and 0% for July 2003 to September 2003.

If the complainant was aggrieved by non-payment of incentive at the agreed upon rate, he has not placed on record any independent evidence to show the steps accordingly taken by him like issuance of notice/ any communication in writing to the accused or Sakida Financial at any stage during his employment and even thereafter stating his grievances and demanding payment of the incentive amount.

Any reasonable man who over a period of approximately one year has not been paid the incentives he is entitled to, is expected to take certain steps like a notice/email/written communication in writing to his employer/senior management in this regard.

Even for the sake of argument, if it is considered that the accused did not pay any heed to the demand of the complainant and also maltreated him in the presence of office staff, the latter could have apprised any other person in the position of authority regarding the behaviour being meted out to him and his grievances but no such steps were taken.
27.

Further, the fact that no rate at which incentive amount has to be paid is mentioned on the appointment letter Ex. PW 1/2 combined with the fact incentive was awarded at different rates during one year of complainant's KATYAYINI by KATYAYINI SHARMA KANDWAL KANDWAL Date: 2024.07.15 16:26:26 +0530 employment with Sakida Financial gives credibility to the claim of the accused that no rate of incentive was agreed upon between the parties and it depended upon various other factors.

28. Moreover, there is not an iota of evidence on record to show that there was deduction of provident fund from the salary of the complainant or that the accused had dishonestly misappropriated or converted to his own use that amount, or dishonestly used or disposed of that amount or wilfully suffered any other person to do so.

Even the fact that the salary for the month of September 2003 was not paid to the complainant finds support in the fact that the complainant did not serve the notice period as mentioned in appointment letter Ex. PW 1/2 which clearly stated that the employment can be terminated by either party by giving one month/s notice in writing.

Since,
Pawan Gupta vs Sanjeev Mahajan on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/178291896/
8

no further written documentation between the parties in the form of employment agreement etc.
has been brought on record, it can be presumed that the terms of employment of the complainant with Sakida Financial continued to be governed by the terms and conditions as laid down in Ex. PW 1/2.

It has been admitted by the complainant that he left his job without serving any notice upon the employer and hence, any company would be entitled to deduct salary of one month where notice period is not served by the employee unless amicably agreed upon otherwise between them.
Even otherwise, at the very best, this can be categorized as a civil dispute between the parties for breach of an agreement and not a criminal dispute.
29. Therefore, this Court is of the view that commission of offence punishable under section 406 of the IPC is not made out in the present case.

CRIMINAL INTIMIDATION 30. Section 506 provides punishment for criminal intimidation which is defined in section 503 of the IPC as follows:
KATYAYINI by KATYAYINI SHARMA KANDWAL KANDWAL Date: 2024.07.15 16:26:37 +0530 Whoever threatens another with any injury to his person, reputation or property, or to the person or reputation of any one in whom that person is interested, with intent to cause alarm to that person, or to cause that person to do any act which he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do any act which that person is legally entitled to do, as the means of avoiding the execution of such threat, commits criminal intimidation.
Explanation.--
A threat to injure the reputation of any deceased person in whom the person threatened is interested, is within this section.
31. Threat to cause death or grievous hurt is punishable under section 506 part II of the IPC.
The case of the complainant is that the accused along with two persons came to his office, slapped him and threatened him to death.

32. In judgment titled Kanshi Ram Vs. State 2000 SCC OnLine Del 385 the Hon'ble Delhi High Court observed as follows:
"So far as the offence under section 506 IPC is concerned, the complainant Israr Ahmed stated in his case diary statement that at the relevant time the petitioner had exhorted his security personnel to thrash the journalists.

entities.text: Kanshi Ram Vs. State 2000 SCC OnLine Del 385
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
According to Israr Ahmed,
the exact words used by the petitioner were "Maro Salon Ko".
Strangely enough, Israr Ahmed has nowhere stated in his statement that the alleged threat had caused an alarm to him.
On the contrary, the circumstances of the case clearly go to show that even after the alleged threat, the complainant or other media persons did not retrace their steps.
It is well-settled that mere threat is no offence.

That being so, the threat alleged to have been given by the petitioner KATYAYINI by KATYAYINI SHARMA Pawan Gupta vs Sanjeev Mahajan on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/178291896/

entities.text: KATYAYINI SHARMA Pawan Gupta vs Sanjeev Mahajan on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 9 KANDWAL KANDWAL Date: 2024.07.15 16:26:48 +0530 does not fall within the mischief of Section 506 IPC.
Consequently, no charge under section 506 IPC can be framed against the petitioner on the basis of the said evidence."

33. In judgment titled Surinder Suri Vs State of Haryana 1996 SCC OnLine P&H 582, the Hon'ble Punjab and Haryana High Court has observed as follows:
"The gist of the offence is the effect which the threat is intended to have upon the mind of the person threatened. The threat must be one which can be put into execution by the person threatening.

entities.text: Surinder Suri Vs State of Haryana 1996 SCC OnLine P&H 582
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: A threat, in order to be indictable must be made with intent to cause alarm to the complainant.

As for instance, mere vague allegations by the accused that he is going to take revenge by false complaints cannot amount to criminal intimidation".
34.

Infact, recently in Sugurappa and Others v. State of Karanataka 2023 SCC OnLine Kar 165,
Hon'ble Karnataka High Court also held that:
"to constitute offence of criminal intimidation, there must be threat with intention to cause alarm to the complainant or to do any act which is not legally bound to do.

entities.text: Sugurappa and Others v. State of Karanataka 2023 SCC OnLine Kar 165
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Mere expression of any words without any intention to cause alarm to the complainant or to make him to do, or omit to do any act, is not sufficient to bring the act within the definition of criminal intimidation."
35.
Thus, it is no more res integra that in order to prove the offence under Section 506, IPC, there must be evidence to show that the complainant was alarmed by the threats advanced by the accused.
In the present case, there is not even an iota of evidence to prove that the complainant was alarmed by any threat advanced by the accused, if at all any such threats were ever advanced.
No independent witness has been KATYAYINI by KATYAYINI SHARMA SHARMA KANDWAL KANDWAL
Date: 2024.07.15 16:27:02 +0530 examined by the complainant in support of his testimony.

In fact, even the exact words allegedly uttered by the accused to the complainant have been mentioned anywhere in the testimony of the complainant, in order to enable the court to determine the intent behind utterance of such words.

Therefore, this Court is of the opinion that the accused cannot be convicted for the offence punishable under Section 506, IPC.
36.
It is important to underscore the established canon of criminal law that in order to pass a conviction in a criminal case, the accused "must be" guilty and not merely "may be" guilty.

The mental distance between "may be"
guilty to "must be" guilty is a long one and must be travel not on surmises and conjectures, but by cogent evidence.
As per law, an accused is not required to prove his defence beyond all reasonable doubts.
It is sufficient if he proves his defence on the preponderance of probabilities.
In the present case, the accused has successfully been able to raise reasonable doubt in the version of the complainant.

As per the settled law, this is all that what is required, as preponderance of probabilities is not a Pawan Gupta vs Sanjeev Mahajan on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/178291896/
10
rigorous standard of proof, but only so much evidence as makes the court lean in favour of one side and not the other.
Consequently, the benefit of doubt must go to the accused.

The material on record does not suggest that the accused "must be"
guilty whichever way one looks at it.
37. It is also settled proposition of law that whenever there are two views possible, the view which favours the innocence of the accused has to be accepted by the Court.
In the present case, as discussed hereinabove, reasonable doubts have been raised by the defence on the case of the complainant.
It would not be safe to convict the accused in the present case without corroborating statement of any independent witness.
Therefore, benefit of reasonable doubts is to be given to the accused as per law.
KATYAYINI by KATYAYINI
SHARMA KANDWAL  KANDWAL
In light of foregoing reasons, this Court accordingly returns a finding of not guilty against the accused Sanjeev Mahajan.

The accused is hereby acquitted for the offence as punishable under 323/406/506 Part II IPC.
39.

13. Ld. Counsel for complainant while relying on judgment in State v. Abdul Rehman and Anr. in Crl. Case No. 4/2023 passed by Ld. ACMM-04, Rouse Avenue Courts, New Delhi dated 29.04.2023,
has stated that the testimony of complainant as CW-1 is sufficient to prove commission of offence punishable under section 323 of the IPC.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Simply because there is statement of only one witness is not sufficient to discredit the testimony without considering the complete facts and circumstances of the case.
However, in the present case, this Court is of the opinion that the complainant has not been able to prove commission of offence under section 323 of the IPC.
No complaint qua alleged incident was registered by him with the police and no notice has been issued to the accused.
It is reasonable that rate of incentive, unless clearly agreed upon, would depend on not only the business accrued by an employee but also the profits accrued to the company.
Moreover, the complainant has not been able to lead any independent evidence in support of his claim.
As per section 103 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the burden of proof lies on the person who alleges some new facts.
Merely because incentive at the rate of 0.53% was paid for the business of October and November 2002 does not imply that the given percentage was agreed upon as the fixed rate of incentive.
Even the fact that the salary for the month of September 2003 was not paid to the complainant finds support in the fact that the complainant did not serve the notice period as mentioned in appointment letter Ex. PW 1/2 which clearly stated that the employment can be terminated by either party by giving one month/s notice in writing.
Since,
Pawan Gupta vs Sanjeev Mahajan on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/178291896/
8
no further written documentation between the parties in the form of employment agreement etc.
has been brought on record, it can be presumed that the terms of employment of the complainant with Sakida Financial continued to be governed by the terms and conditions as laid down in Ex. PW 1/2.
It has been admitted by the complainant that he left his job without serving any notice upon the employer and hence, any company would be entitled to deduct salary of one month where notice period is not served by the employee unless amicably agreed upon otherwise between them.
Even otherwise, at the very best, this can be categorized as a civil dispute between the parties for breach of an agreement and not a criminal dispute.
Thus, it is no more res integra that in order to prove the offence under Section 506, IPC, there must be evidence to show that the complainant was alarmed by the threats advanced by the accused.
In the present case, there is not even an iota of evidence to prove that the complainant was alarmed by any threat advanced by the accused, if at all any such threats were ever advanced.
In fact, even the exact words allegedly uttered by the accused to the complainant have been mentioned anywhere in the testimony of the complainant, in order to enable the court to determine the intent behind utterance of such words.
Therefore, this Court is of the opinion that the accused cannot be convicted for the offence punishable under Section 506, IPC.
36.
It is important to underscore the established canon of criminal law that in order to pass a conviction in a criminal case, the accused "must be" guilty and not merely "may be" guilty.
The mental distance between "may be"
guilty to "must be" guilty is a long one and must be travel not on surmises and conjectures, but by cogent evidence.
As per law, an accused is not required to prove his defence beyond all reasonable doubts.
It is sufficient if he proves his defence on the preponderance of probabilities.
In the present case, the accused has successfully been able to raise reasonable doubt in the version of the complainant.
Consequently, the benefit of doubt must go to the accused.
The material on record does not suggest that the accused "must be"
guilty whichever way one looks at it.
It would not be safe to convict the accused in the present case without corroborating statement of any independent witness.
Therefore, benefit of reasonable doubts is to be given to the accused as per law.
opennyai_summary.decision:
In light of foregoing reasons, this Court accordingly returns a finding of not guilty against the accused Sanjeev Mahajan.
The accused is hereby acquitted for the offence as punishable under 323/406/506 Part II IPC.
